# Beta Pegasi: A Long-Period Variable

*SIMBAD’s catalog entries give a starting point for finding and following this star—but not a schedule for its changing light.*

Beta Pegasi is identified in SIMBAD as a long-period variable. That label makes it more than a point to locate: it is a star to revisit. The catalog supplies a position, a parallax, a spectral type and a visual magnitude, but it does not give a period or a brightness range in the record cited here. So the best observing plan is a patient one: look, make a note, and return.

SIMBAD lists the star’s J2000 coordinates as right ascension 23 hours 03 minutes 46.46 seconds and declination +28 degrees 04 minutes 58.03 seconds. Its identifier is HIP 113881, and the database associates it with “bet Peg.” The coordinates are a precise way to identify the target on a star chart or in an observing app. They also place it north of the celestial equator, at a declination of about 28 degrees. [SIMBAD lists the coordinates and identification here.](https://simbad.cds.unistra.fr/simbad/sim-id?Ident=HIP%20113881)

The same record gives a parallax of 16.64 milliarcseconds. Converting that value gives a distance of about 60 parsecs, or roughly 196 light-years. These are calculated approximations from the cataloged parallax, not separate distance measurements quoted in the record. SIMBAD also lists a spectral type of M2.5 II–III. That designation is a compact classification attached to the star; it is another useful point of comparison when looking up Beta Pegasi in astronomical references.

For brightness, the record lists a visual magnitude of 2.42. Because SIMBAD classifies the star as variable, that catalog entry should be treated as a reference value—not as a promise that the star will appear exactly that bright on a particular observing night. The supplied record does not state how far its brightness varies or how long a cycle takes. It therefore cannot tell an observer when to expect a noticeable change.

A modest observing project can fill in a different kind of record: your own. Find Beta Pegasi using its catalog designation or coordinates, then write down the date, time and observing conditions. Add a careful estimate of its brightness. If you repeat the observation, use the same approach each time and note any differences you perceive. Comparing its appearance with other stars can help make estimates
